name: Adze-Scar
description: Adze-Scar looks as though something took a cosmic adze to its surface and carved away a quarter of the planet. A catastrophic impact in the distant past gouged out a basin so deep it exposed the partially solidified core, leaving a world that is essentially a geological cross-section. The remaining surface is a maze of canyon systems radiating outward from the impact basin like cracks in shattered glass, their walls exposing rich veins of platinum-group metals that gleam in the unfiltered starlight.

Without atmosphere, the transition between brutal sunlight and absolute darkness is instantaneous at every canyon edge. The exposed core material glows with a dull, ruddy heat that is visible from orbit on the nightside, a wound that has never fully healed. Temperature extremes are savage, and the thermal cycling has shattered the canyon walls into unstable scree slopes that shift without warning, making surface operations treacherous.

A mining consortium established operations here during the platinum rush, building a pressurized complex along the richest veins. The operation collapsed when a core tremor triggered a canyon wall failure that buried half the complex. The evacuation was chaotic, and an escape pod debris field marks the trajectory of the survivors' desperate flight. Not all pods were recovered, and at least two are believed to have fallen back into the exposed core basin.

The platinum deposits remain among the richest known, and the exposed core offers unique research opportunities in planetary geology. But the site is unstable, with core tremors increasing in frequency and intensity. New surveys suggest the ancient impact may have fractured the core itself, and the planet may be slowly breaking apart along the radial canyon lines. Any future mining operation faces a literal race against geological time.
